title: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is ‘unpatchable’
content:
During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited.
“Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.”
In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches.
The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FFA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation.
Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.”
“We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added.
“Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure … and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.”
Nadella made a broader point as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems.
“We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made sophisticated cyberattacks much easier to enact.
“The patch [now] needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild, right? So that’s going to create instability.”

report.summary: Nadella warns many internet-connected critical infrastructure systems have unpatchable firmware, while AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
report.background: The warning comes as cheap connectivity and industrial IoT have pushed once-isolated devices—firmware, chillers, HVAC systems, transportation gear—onto the public internet. Many were designed without update mechanisms or long-term security support, creating a large legacy attack surface. At the same time, AI is changing both sides of the security race: it helps defenders find bugs at scale, but also lowers the cost of sophisticated exploitation. Recent high-profile outages, including Microsoft Outlook and systems tied to government agencies, have heightened concerns, even as officials have denied some were cyberattacks. Nadella's remarks at the DealBook Summit reflect a broader industry shift toward secure-by-design modernization, faster patch deployment, and real-time detection as AI-assisted attacks compress response windows.
key_points: Nadella singled out firmware, data-center chillers, HVAC systems and transportation equipment as examples of critical infrastructure that is often internet-connected but cannot be patched. That reflects a decade-long smartification push that added connectivity to devices never designed for remote updates or modern security support, leaving a broad legacy attack surface.

He argued AI has created a powerful vulnerability-discovery tool, but also made sophisticated attacks easier. The result is a compressed patch window: fixes must move from release to production almost instantly because exploits are already in the wild, which can itself create operational instability.

The comments followed recent large-scale outages, including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Nadella described the Outlook incident as a latent bug that became a perfect storm, and said Microsoft will apply architectural and operational lessons. Other outages have raised cyberattack fears, though officials have denied some claims.

Nadella called for modernizing vulnerable systems and assessing threat vectors, detection and real-time defense. The implication is that patching alone cannot secure exposed legacy gear; organizations need inventory, segmentation, monitoring and replacement strategies for unpatchable components, especially as AI-assisted attacks scale.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Nadella's warning underscores the dual-use nature of security models: the same automation that finds bugs can accelerate exploitation, so vendors will face pressure to build secure-by-design systems and guardrails. Developers should expect more emphasis on SBOMs, firmware signing, dependency scanning, rapid patch pipelines and AI-assisted code review—plus observability for devices that cannot be updated. Regular users may see more outages and service disruptions as exposed infrastructure is probed; the risk is highest for utilities, transport and data centers, but better inventory and segmentation can reduce blast radius. The bigger shift is from periodic patching to continuous risk management.
report.tools: For follow-up, watch CISA's KEV catalog for exploited vulnerabilities, OpenSSF Scorecard and OSV for dependency risk, and Syft/Grype plus Dependency-Track for SBOM and vulnerability tracking. Semgrep and Nuclei help scan code and exposed services; Garak supports LLM red-teaming. Microsoft's Secure Future Initiative is also worth tracking for patch-automation and secure-by-design practices.
